Joel 1.summary: The book opens by identifying the prophetic word as coming to Joel, son of Pethuel (Joel 1:1), but supplies no king or date. Joel summons elders and all inhabitants to remember and tell succeeding generations about an overwhelming calamity (Joel 1:2–3). Successive kinds or stages of locusts have consumed the crops (Joel 1:4); the devastation is described with imagery of an invading nation with lionlike teeth (Joel 1:6–7). Drinkers, farmers, vine dressers, and priests mourn because grain, wine, oil, and the produce of the land have failed (Joel 1:5–12). The shortage disrupts the grain and drink offerings at the house of the LORD (Joel 1:9, 13). Joel calls priests to lament, proclaim a fast, and convene a solemn assembly to cry out to God (Joel 1:13–14). He names the approaching “day of the LORD” as a time of destruction (Joel 1:15). The chapter ends with the prophet's cry to God as food, pasture, trees, and streams suffer, and even wild animals pant for water (Joel 1:16–20). Joel gives no date for the disaster; his point is that a crisis this size calls for serious lament and a collective turning back to God.
Joel 1.whereWeAre: Hosea ended with a call for Israel to return to the LORD and a promise that God would heal their unfaithfulness (Hosea 14:1–9). Joel opens the next book with a different crisis: a locust plague and drought so severe that even the grain and drink offerings at the temple have stopped. The prophet summons the whole community to mourn and declare a fast, setting up his warning in chapter 2 that this disaster is only a sign of the greater “day of the LORD” still to come.

keyFigures.name: Joel son of Pethuel
keyFigures.role: Named prophet and poetic speaker. Reports the divine word and calls the people to lament (1:1, 13–20)

keyFigures.name: Elders and inhabitants of the land
keyFigures.role: Hearers addressed by Joel. Must preserve the memory of the calamity and respond (1:2–3, 14)

keyFigures.name: Priests and ministers of the altar
keyFigures.role: Temple servants. Called to mourn, fast, and assemble the people because offerings have ceased (1:9, 13–14)

keyFigures.name: Farmers, vine dressers, and those who drink wine
keyFigures.role: Affected community groups. Show how the crop destruction disrupts daily life and livelihood (1:5, 11–12)

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: God addressed and announced in the prophecy. Receives the prayer and is associated with the coming day of judgment (1:14–15, 19)

keyThemes.theme: Shared suffering and the memory of disaster
keyThemes.explanation: Joel tells the elders to pass this disaster down to their children and grandchildren, since living through something this severe together becomes part of the community's own memory of God's dealings with it (1:2-3).
Wine, grain, and fruit trees that everyone depended on for daily life disappear almost overnight, showing how quickly comfort and security can be stripped away (1:5-12).

With no grain or wine left to bring, the regular offerings at the temple stop; Joel calls the priests to lead a fast and solemn assembly instead, since worship must continue even when the usual gifts cannot be given (1:9-14).

keyThemes.theme: The day of the LORD and lament
keyThemes.explanation: Joel reads the locust plague and drought as a warning sign of a greater reckoning still to come, and responds by crying out to God rather than despairing (1:15-20).

Joel 2.summary: Joel orders a trumpet alarm in Zion because the day of the LORD is near (Joel 2:1). He depicts an unstoppable, army-like force: darkness surrounds it, the land changes from gardenlike fertility to waste, and its advance resembles horses, chariots, and disciplined soldiers (Joel 2:2–11). The imagery may extend the locust plague into something larger, picture a human army, or deliberately combine both into one picture of unstoppable judgment. Yet judgment is not the final appeal: God calls the people to return with all their heart, fasting, weeping, and mourning, and to “rend your heart, and not your garments” (Joel 2:12–13). Joel summons all ages and social groups, including newly married couples, to assembly while priests plead for mercy (Joel 2:15–17). The text then describes the LORD's compassion, removal of the threatening force, renewal of the land, and restoration of grain, wine, and oil; the people will praise God and recognize the LORD in their midst (Joel 2:18–27). Finally, God promises to pour out the Spirit on sons and daughters, old and young, and male and female servants (Joel 2:28–29), accompanied by cosmic signs before the day of the LORD and a promise of deliverance for those who call on God's name (Joel 2:30–32). The chapter connects sincere repentance, promised restoration, and wider participation in God's Spirit, a promise the New Testament identifies with the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21).
Joel 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 described the locust plague's damage and Joel's call for the community to mourn and fast (Joel 1:1–20). Chapter 2 sounds a trumpet alarm and pictures the coming destruction in the most vivid terms in the book, then turns from warning to hope: God calls the people to heartfelt repentance and promises to restore the land and pour out his Spirit on everyone, a promise Peter later quotes at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21). That promise of deliverance sets up chapter 3, where the LORD turns from restoring Judah to judging the nations that wronged it.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaker and actor within the prophetic message. Calls for heartfelt return, promises restoration, and announces the outpouring of the Spirit (2:12–14, 18–32)

keyFigures.name: People of Zion (Judah and Jerusalem)
keyFigures.role: Community receiving the alarm and the call to assembly. Urged to return and later promised renewal (2:1, 15–17, 23–27)

keyFigures.name: Priests and ministers of the LORD
keyFigures.role: Representatives in public worship. Directed to weep between the porch and altar and petition God for the people (2:17)

keyFigures.name: Children, elders, bridegroom, and bride
keyFigures.role: Groups explicitly summoned to communal assembly. Their inclusion underscores that the whole community is involved (2:16)

keyFigures.name: Sons, daughters, old men, young men, servants, and handmaids
keyFigures.role: Recipients named in the promised outpouring. Illustrate the promise extending across sex, age, and status (2:28–29)

keyFigures.name: Northern army
keyFigures.role: Threatening force described in prophetic imagery. Its removal accompanies the announcement of compassion and restoration (2:20)

keyThemes.theme: The day of the LORD and urgent warning
keyThemes.explanation: Joel sounds a trumpet alarm and pictures an overwhelming force sweeping the land bare, framing the advancing danger as proof that the day of the LORD is close and unstoppable (2:1-11).
God calls for inward change, not only the outward signs of mourning, and summons every person in the community, even newlyweds, to the fast (2:12-17).
Once the people turn back, the LORD responds with pity, driving off the destroying force and restoring the very years of harvest the locusts had eaten (2:18-27).

keyThemes.theme: The Spirit shared across the community
keyThemes.explanation: God promises to pour out his Spirit without regard to age, sex, or social status, a promise Peter later applies to the day of Pentecost (2:28-29).

keyThemes.theme: Calling on the LORD amid judgment
keyThemes.explanation: Alongside cosmic signs announcing the day of the LORD, Joel promises that anyone who calls on the LORD's name, not only a select few, will be saved (2:30-32).

explainedReferences.explanation: Prophecy that God will pour out his Spirit and sons and daughters will prophesy; Peter quotes it at Pentecost.
Promise of the Spirit being poured upon male and female servants.
Prediction of wonders involving blood, fire, and smoke.
Description of the sun becoming dark and the moon becoming blood before the day of the Lord.
The first declaration in Joel 2:32 that whoever calls on the Lord's name will be saved.
The declaration that whoever calls on the Lord will be saved.

Joel 3.summary: The final chapter moves from Judah's promised restoration to the LORD's judgment of the nations (Joel 3:1–2). God summons nations to the “valley of Jehoshaphat” because, according to the oracle, they scattered Israel, divided the land, cast lots for people, and traded children (Joel 3:2–3). Tyre, Sidon, and Philistine districts are accused of taking treasures and selling Judahites and Jerusalemites to Greeks; the prophetic speech announces a reversal of their actions (Joel 3:4–8). The nations are ironically commanded to prepare for war, even turning plowshares into swords, and to assemble for judgment (Joel 3:9–12). Harvest and winepress imagery express the fullness of wickedness and impending reckoning (Joel 3:13), while cosmic darkness accompanies the nearness of the day of the LORD (Joel 3:14–15). Yet the LORD is described as a refuge for his people and a stronghold for Israel, dwelling in Zion (Joel 3:16–17). The chapter closes with images of abundant wine, milk, water flowing from God's house, and enduring habitation in Judah and Jerusalem, set against desolation announced for Egypt and Edom (Joel 3:18–21). The chapter's central contrast is judgment on the nations that wronged God's people and lasting hope for Zion that outlasts the locusts and armies described in chapters 1–2.
Joel 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 ended with the LORD's promise to pour out his Spirit on all people and save everyone who calls on his name (Joel 2:28–32). Chapter 3 turns from Judah's restoration to the LORD's judgment of the nations that scattered Israel and sold its people into slavery, gathering them for sentencing in the valley of Jehoshaphat. The book closes with the LORD dwelling in Zion forever, completing Joel's picture of judgment and restoration before Amos, the next book, turns to the LORD's judgment on Israel and its neighbors in greater detail.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Divine judge and refuge proclaimed by the prophet. Calls nations to account and promises to dwell in Zion (3:2, 12, 16–17, 21)

keyFigures.name: Israel, Judah, and Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: The people and places at the center of the oracle. Portrayed as harmed by other nations and later restored (3:1–3, 16–21)

keyFigures.name: The nations
keyFigures.role: Collective parties summoned for judgment. Charged with scattering people and dividing land (3:2–3, 9–14)

keyFigures.name: Tyre, Sidon, and Philistine regions
keyFigures.role: Named neighboring peoples and places. Accused within the oracle of seizure of goods and human trafficking (3:4–8)

keyFigures.name: Greeks and Sabeans
keyFigures.role: Groups mentioned in trade and reversal imagery. Greeks are named as buyers of exiles; Sabeans appear in the announced retaliatory sale (3:6, 8)

keyFigures.name: Egypt and Edom
keyFigures.role: Named nations in the closing oracle. Their desolation is contrasted with Judah’s enduring habitation (3:19–20)

keyThemes.explanation: The LORD charges the nations with scattering his people, dividing their land, and selling children for the price of wine or a prostitute, and promises to return the same treatment on their own heads (3:1-8).

keyThemes.theme: The day of the LORD as judgment
keyThemes.explanation: Joel ironically summons the nations to arm themselves for war, since gathering for battle only brings them to the harvest and winepress of God's judgment (3:9-15).

keyThemes.theme: God as refuge for his people
keyThemes.explanation: Even as the earth shakes, the LORD is described as a shelter and stronghold for Israel, dwelling in Zion rather than abandoning his people (3:16-17).
The book closes with pictures of overflowing abundance and a spring flowing from God's house, promising that Judah and Jerusalem will endure forever because the LORD dwells there (3:18-21).
